title: Abiotic sugar enantiomers in the CI carbonaceous chondrite Orgueil

paper_content.abstract: The uneventful detection of prebiotic organic compounds in meteorites—where amino acids and nucleobases are commonly identified but sugars remain rare and poorly characterized—limits our understanding of extraterrestrial organic chemistry. This discrepancy is striking given that laboratory simulations of interstellar ice chemistry readily produce complex sugars. Here we report the simultaneous analysis of sugar and amino acid enantiomers in a meteorite sample. Multiple aldoses were detected in the Orgueil meteorite, including ribose, arabinose, xylose, lyxose, and the ketopentose ribulose, several of which display near-racemic distributions consistent with an extraterrestrial origin. Recovery experiments demonstrate that sugar abundances are severely underestimated. Despite this limitation, pentose abundances are comparable to those of some C4–C5 amino acid enantiomers, implying higher true concentrations. These results indicate efficient abiotic sugar formation in space and suggest that meteorites may have delivered a broader range of prebiotically relevant sugars to early Earth than previously recognized.
paper_content.introduction:
Nucleic acids (RNA, DNA), composed of sugars, nucleobases, and phosphates, and proteins, built from amino acids, are the fundamental biopolymers of life. A central question concerning the origin of life on Earth is how these essential biomolecular building blocks were synthesized, concentrated, and assembled into biopolymers, given their fragile nature, the planet’s extreme and fluctuating environmental conditions1–3 and the brief timescale for life’s emergence following Earth’s consolidation4. One plausible source of these biomolecular precursors to the terrestrial prebiotic inventory, strongly supported by both astronomical and geological evidence, is their exogenous delivery via extraterrestrial bodies such as interplanetary dust particles and meteorites1,5–10, supplementing the local prebiotic synthesis on early Earth.

However, while amino acids and nucleobases have been repeatedly detected in various carbonaceous chondrites11–14 and, more recently, in samples from the asteroids Ryugu15–17 and Bennu18, the detection of sugars—essential as components of nucleic acids but also as monomers of structural and energy‑storage polymers in all living organisms—remains remarkably scarce. To date, only a single study by Furukawa et al.19 has confirmed the presence of ribose and other aldopentoses in meteorite samples, highlighting the current limitations in our ability to detect and understand sugar inventories in extraterrestrial materials. Moreover, the relatively large sample masses required in that study (~2 g) further constrain the applicability of such analyses to scarce pristine materials such as those returned from asteroids (Ryugu, total=5.4 g; Bennu, 121.6 g). However, sugars and sugar-related compounds have recently been identified in powdered aliquots of regolith returned from asteroid Bennu by the OSIRIS-REx mission20 (OREX-800107-108; 603.4 mg), demonstrating that such compounds can be detected in substantially smaller masses of pristine asteroidal material. Nevertheless, the paucity of data on extraterrestrial sugars contrasts sharply with numerous laboratory studies on interstellar ice21–24 and planetary or parent body mineral analogs25–27, which predict the widespread formation of a diverse range of C3 to C6 aldose sugars under extraterrestrial conditions. Moreover, glycolaldehyde, a potential precursor of larger carbohydrates, has been previously detected in the interstellar medium towards the Galactic center source Sagittarius B2(N)28 as well as on comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko29. From a prebiotic chemistry perspective, investigating the presence, abundance, and formation mechanisms of sugars under astrophysical conditions is a critical objective. Indeed, the potential delivery of sugars like ribose via meteorites could have provided a sustained source for the formation of primitive nucleotides in environments such as warm little ponds that may have facilitated their stabilization through rapid polymerization2. This is particularly significant given the inherent instability of sugars in aqueous environments6,30–33, where rapid degradation could otherwise limit their role in early biochemical pathways. The apparent scarcity of sugars in extraterrestrial samples has been attributed to their potential chemical transformation in space or within the meteorite mineral matrix, where they may be converted into sugar alcohols or sugar acids34. In addition, strong matrix effects—particularly the entrapment of sugars within clay mineral phases—could significantly reduce extraction efficiencies35,36.

A major challenge in analyzing prebiotically relevant organics such as amino acids and sugars from astrophysical samples lies in confirming their extraterrestrial origin, due to the ever-present risk of terrestrial contamination. While meteorites are often subject to terrestrial weathering and potential microbial colonization prior to analysis37,38, even returned samples—such as those from (162173) Ryugu and (101955) Bennu, despite being collected under meticulously controlled conditions by the JAXA’s Hayabusa2 and NASA’s OSIRIS-REx missions38–41 require meticulous handling and verification protocols to confidently assess indigenous organics. Contamination risks remain particularly relevant during post-collection sample processing37. Stable isotope ratios provide a powerful tool for addressing this issue, as they yield insights into the formation pathways and environmental conditions of organic compounds. Importantly, they can help distinguish biological from abiotic origins, since extraterrestrial organics are typically enriched in heavy isotopes relative to their terrestrial counterparts11,42. Notably, chiral amino acids found in meteorites have been found to be enriched in the heavy isotopes 13C, 15N, and D (deuterium)43–45. Similarly, the 13C isotopic enrichment of the detected sugars in Murchison (CM2) and NWA 801 (CR2) meteorites was used to support their extraterrestrial origin19. However, the feasibility and precision of compound-specific isotopic measurements are significantly constrained by the need for high analyte concentrations, requiring large sample sizes46. This constraint makes isotopic analysis of soluble organics impossible for many relevant extraterrestrial samples, for which very limited sample material is available. Furthermore, since isotopic measurements depend on prior chromatographic separations, the sample preparation process can introduce additional losses and analytical biases, further compromising the reliability of the measurements46. In particular, in the only confirmed detection of sugars in meteorites, Furukawa et al.19 reported that the accuracy of the carbon isotope measurements for arabinose in NWA 801 was limited by a significant co-eluting peak, preventing reliable δ13C determination.

As a result of this limitation, enantiomeric excess measurements of chiral organics have increasingly become crucial for evaluating terrestrial contamination, particularly in samples of limited mass available for analysis13,38. The molecular architecture of life on Earth is defined by a striking preference for specific chiral configurations—such as L-amino acids in proteins and D-sugars in nucleic acids—therefore, near-racemic mixtures or the presence of non-biological enantiomers suggest abiotic, and potentially extraterrestrial, origins.

In this study, we report the detection and enantiomeric separation of all four aldopentoses and ribulose, a ketopentose, in a fragment of the Orgueil carbonaceous meteorite weighing only 178 mg. Our analysis combined ultrasound-assisted extraction, ion-exchange chromatography for fractionation and purification, with enantioselective comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography coupled to time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC–TOF‑MS)47,48. The differences in enantiomeric distributions between the detected sugars and the procedural blanks, along with the near-racemic distribution of ribulose, provide evidence supporting their possible extraterrestrial origin.

Critically, enantiomeric resolution was essential for confirming the origin of the detected sugars, as the limited quantities targeted precluded isotopic analysis. Our findings challenge the widely held assumption that sugars are significantly less abundant than amino acids in carbonaceous chondrites. Incorporating compound-specific recovery rates indicates that the estimated quantities of individual sugar enantiomers are at least comparable to those of C4–C5 amino acid enantiomers in the same samples. These results support the hypothesis that meteorites delivered not only amino acids and nucleobases but also appreciable amounts of prebiotic sugars to early Earth—bridging a critical gap between their abiotic synthesis in interstellar ices and their potential role in the emergence of early biochemical systems.
paper_content.results:
To characterize the sugar and amino acid content of the Orgueil sample while minimizing the degradation of labile organics, we developed an analytical workflow combining sequential extraction, fractionation, and derivatization steps optimized for the simultaneous recovery and separate enantioselective analysis of both compound classes (Fig. 1). Key to this methodology is a mild extraction protocol employing ultrasonic-assisted extraction (temperature <20 °C, neutral pH, and 10-min sonication intervals) to prevent thermal degradation of sugars32. An ion exchange chromatography (IEC) step was employed to remove inorganic ions (e.g., Fe2+, Fe3+, and Mg2+)—major components of chondritic mineral matrices that interfere with subsequent derivatization and chromatographic protocols49,50—and to separate neutral sugars from amino acid zwitterions49. This separation allows for tailored derivatization procedures and chromatographic conditions specific to each molecular class, enhancing both sensitivity and selectivity in their analyses. A detailed description of the sample preparation, extraction procedure, and chromatographic measurements is in the “Methods” section.

Detection of ribulose and aldopentoses in Orgueil
Building on the reported inverse relationship between sugar-related compound abundance and carbon number reported by Cooper et al.34, we focused on the detection of C3 to C5 sugar aldoses, including glyceraldehyde, erythrose, ribose, 2-deoxyribose, lyxose, arabinose, xylose, as well as the C5 ketose ribulose. These compounds were targeted as methylboronic acid derivatives using GC×GC–TOF-MS, chosen for its high enantiomeric resolution power and detectability47. Despite the limited sample quantity of 178.3 mg of meteorite material and the challenges associated with the extraction and analysis of sugars from extraterrestrial samples we unambiguously detected all four C5 aldoses at concentrations above procedural blank levels (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 4). A detailed comparison of sugar enantiomers in the Orgueil sample and procedural blanks is provided in Supplementary Figs. 4–5 alongside their corresponding mass spectra (Supplementary Figs. 6–9). Arabinose and xylose detected in Orgueil exhibited much stronger biases towards the biologically abundant enantiomers L-arabinose and D-xylose, likely resulting at least partly from terrestrial contamination accumulated over the long curation history of this CI meteorite51. In contrast to arabinose and xylose, the prebiotically significant sugar ribose and its rare stereoisomer lyxose were both detected in nearly racemic proportions (Fig. 2), suggesting an abiotic origin.

Enantiomeric excess (ee) data for arabinose and xylose in the Orgueil sample are reported in Table 1. For the other detected sugars, rapid degradation of their derivatives in the presence of residual matrix material (Supplementary Fig. 10) hindered replicate analyses, rendering the corresponding ee values indicative rather than statistically robust. The %ee calculations were based on the peak areas of both enantiomers in the single ion chromatograms to minimize uncertainties associated with calibration curves, such as the conversion from ion counts to ppb. Moreover, matrix effects likely cause different slopes between standard and meteoritic sample curves, potentially leading to inaccurate concentrations. The same approach was applied for the amino acids reported below.

We also report the detection of the C5 ketose ribulose, found in near-racemic proportions. Figure 3 shows the GC×GC chromatograms and corresponding mass spectra of the ribulose enantiomers, along with procedural blanks and reference standards for comparison.

The concentrations of sugars measured in the Orgueil sample ranged from 0.1 to 6.8 ppb, corresponding to approximately 0.67 to 45 pmol/g (Table 1). Arabinose and xylose concentrations were 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than those reported for the CM2 meteorite Murchison by Furukawa et al.19. However, because the reported isotopic ratio of Murchison xylose (δ13C ≈ −1 ± 4‰) falls only slightly outside the terrestrial range (−32 to −1‰) and its abundance is relatively high compared with other sugars, a terrestrial contribution to the observed xylose signal cannot be fully excluded, particularly in the absence of enantiomeric resolution. Given the very limited dataset on meteoritic sugars, it is premature to attribute the apparent differences in sugar abundances between CI and CM chondrites to variations in parent-body histories or mineral compositions. Comparison of aldopentose distributions between Orgueil and Bennu20 reveals some quantitative differences that likely reflect either distinct parent-body processing histories or variations in matrix effects during extraction. Lyxose abundances are of the same order of magnitude in both samples, while ribose appears slightly less abundant in Orgueil; these comparisons do not yet account for the low recovery rates in our analyses (~20% for lyxose and ~5% for ribose). In contrast, arabinose and xylose show more substantial differences between Orgueil and Bennu.

To better constrain the origin of the detected sugars, we conducted a detailed assessment of potential contamination sources in our procedural blanks. We compared sugar levels in the reagent blank with those in procedural blanks prepared without and with the SiO2 matrix, which indicated that the major contribution to contamination arose during the derivatization step, specifically from the derivatization reagents (Supplementary Note 2, Supplementary Fig. 4). Moreover, spiking experiments with several milligrams of a previously extracted Orgueil sample revealed a pronounced suppression of sugar recovery in the presence of a CI-type meteorite matrix (Supplementary Note 3), with recovery rates ranging from approximately 1% for ribulose to 30% for arabinose. Notably, these compound-specific recovery efficiencies align with the aldopentoses ultimately detected and plausibly explain the absence of others whose recovery rates were below our detection threshold for the limited sample available for analysis. Importantly, these recovery tests provide evidence of non-uniform behavior among individual aldopentoses, with variable recoveries (Table 1) and degradation patterns (Supplementary Fig. 10) under identical conditions, suggesting sugar-dependent interactions with the sample matrix and/or during analytical processing. This highlights the need for standardized protocols employing closely resembling meteorite matrices in procedural blanks to ensure accurate blank correction when quantifying extraterrestrial abundances and enantiomeric excesses, especially for inter–parent-body comparisons.

Aqueously altered amino acid signatures in Orgueil
We simultaneously analyzed amino acids in the same sample extract to (1) monitor potential biological contamination in the absence of isotopic measurements, (2) evaluate the efficiency of our modified methodology with previous analyses of Orgueil samples, and (3) contextualize sugar abundances relative to better-characterized organic molecules within the same fragment. Given the limited availability of sugar data in the literature, amino acids—abundant and well-documented in Orgueil (Table 2)—served as a valid reference point. A total of 25 amino acids, including proteinogenic, rare, and non-biological types, were detected. The abundances of the identified amino acids are summarized in Table 2 and compared with previously reported data for Orgueil51,52. The concentrations of the most abundant amino acids, glycine and β-alanine, closely align with previous reports, reinforcing their status as characteristic amino acids in CI, CM1, and CR1 meteorites51,52. A similar agreement was observed for C3 and C4 amino acids, except for 4-ABA. However, the C5 amino acids were present at concentrations roughly ten times lower in our extract compared to those reported in previous studies. Our analysis also revealed several amino acids not previously identified in Orgueil, including four proteinogenic amino acids (threonine, proline, leucine, and isoleucine) and six rare amino acids (N-methylglycine, N-ethylglycine, 2,3-DAP, 2,4-DAB, norleucine, and allo-isoleucine).

The distribution of amino acid structural isomers in meteorites varies significantly across different groups, reflecting distinct parent body conditions and alteration histories12,49,53. Orgueil (CI1) samples display markedly lower total amino acid abundances compared to less aqueously altered CM2 (e.g., Murchison) and CR2-CR3 chondrites—a pattern attributed to extensive aqueous processing on their parent bodies54,55. This lower content is particularly pronounced for hydrophilic amino acids, likely resulting from destruction during prolonged aqueous alteration and analytical biases due to phyllosilicate-rich matrices (>90 vol.%), which trap amino acids and reduce extraction efficiencies55. The predominance of glycine and β-alanine aligns with CI chondrite alteration trends, suggesting formation via HCN polymerization and Michael addition in an ice-rich parent body containing ammonia, hydrogen cyanide, and cyanoacetylene52,53.

The enantiomeric ratios of selected chiral amino acids were calculated as L-enantiomeric excess (%eeL) (Table 3) to evaluate potential contamination during the analysis. Alanine and aspartic acid showed rather small L-excesses, while other proteinogenic amino acids (serine and valine) exhibited significant L-excess. This aligns, however, with previous data from Orgueil16,51 (Table 3) where high L-excess for serine/aspartic acid (in unhydrolyzed samples) was reported. The non-proteinogenic amino acids 2-ABA and 3-AIB were found in nearly racemic proportions. Notably, isovaline exhibited minor L-excess, matching reported values for non-hydrolyzed samples51,52.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation
A 178.3 mg fragment of the Orgueil meteorite, of a total of 1.0 g allocated by the Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle (MNHN) in Paris and stored in a plastic container (Supplementary Fig. 1), was analyzed in this study. The fragment was transferred into a pre-weighed 5 mL V-Vial (V-Vial® Wheaton) using clean tweezers inside a Class II laminar flow safety cabinet (Thermo Scientific MSC-Advantage Class II). All glassware was cleaned with 96% ethanol and Milli-Q water, then wrapped in aluminum foil and heated at 500 °C for 5 h. Other labware, including needles, caps, spatulas, tweezers, PTFE frits (20 μm pore size, Supelco), and PTFE disposable liners (Supelco), were thoroughly cleaned with HPLC-grade ethanol and Milli-Q® water, dried with a stream of pure nitrogen, and wrapped in pre-burned aluminum foil until further use. Biopur tips (2–200 μL and 50–1000 μL Eppendorf epT.I.P.S. Biopur) were employed when needed.

Ultrasonic-assisted extraction
Ultrasonic extraction was performed using a Fisherbrand FB15049 (Elma Schmidbauer GmbH, Singen) at a fixed frequency of 37 kHz operating in sweep mode. Prior to extraction, the water bath was degassed for 1 to 5 min to remove entrapped air and dissolved gases. 3D printed holders were employed to fix the position of the vials containing the samples in a reproducible way. The temperature of the bath was maintained between 15 and 21 °C. For high-temperature extractions, an MS-100 Thermo Shaker incubator was employed. Additional instrumentation used for sample pre-treatment, including specifications and operating parameters, is detailed in the Supplementary Note 1.

The extraction protocol applied for analyzing the Orgueil sample is schematically illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 2. A procedural blank (PB), without a matrix, was prepared alongside the sample. Two distinct extracts were obtained: a methanolic (Sigma Aldrich, >99.9%) extract, expected to contain extracted sugars and minor quantities of amino acids, and an aqueous extract, primarily containing amino acids. Subsequently, multiple water (Milli‑Q Direct 8 apparatus, 18.2 MΩ cm at 25 °C, <2 ppb total organic carbon) extraction steps, including conventional hot-water extraction, were performed to enhance amino acid recovery. The detailed water extraction procedure for each step was as follows: 1. Cold methanol extraction (sugar fraction): The Orgueil fragment was crushed with 1.784 mL of methanol (MeOH) using a glass rod to ensure thorough solvent penetration. The sample was then vortex-mixed and sonicated for 10 min at 17–20 °C. After sonication, it was centrifuged at 9500 × g (9000 rpm) for 10 min with a Hettich Universal 320 centrifuge with an angle-fixed rotor model 1620A, and the supernatant was transferred to a 25 mL glass bottle. This extraction process was repeated five times, with all extracts combined into the same 25 mL flask. To minimize the co-evaporation of volatile compounds during pre-concentration under low pressure, 5 mL of water was added to the methanol extracts. The sample was then stored in the fridge at 5 °C until subsequent purification and fractionation. 2a. Cold water extraction: After methanolic extraction, the extraction continued seven more times on the matrix residue, using water instead of methanol. The resulting supernatants were transferred into a separate 25 mL glass bottle. The sample was then stored in the fridge at 5 °C until subsequent purification and fractionation. 2b. Hot water extraction: Next, 3.6 mL of water was added to the 5 mL vial containing the meteorite residue for hot-water extraction at 100 °C for 21 h. The resulting extract was then centrifuged at 9500 × g and combined with the cold-water extracts from step 2a. 2c. Cold water extraction: Three additional cold-water extractions were performed on the remaining matrix using 1.784 mL of water per extraction. The resulting supernatants were combined with the previous aqueous extracts (2a and 2b) for purification and fractionation.

Ion exchange chromatography (IEC)
Purification and fractionation. The methanolic extracts (approximately 15 mL MeOH/H2O (2:1, v/v) were loaded onto the corresponding ion exchange chromatography (IEC) columns in 200 μL portions using a Pasteur pipette (Supplementary Note 1). Eluates were collected in a 25 mL pear-shaped flask. The 25 mL bottles containing the extracts were rinsed with 5 × 0.5 mL of H2O to optimize compound recovery. The rinses were then eluted through the columns and collected in the same 25 mL pear-shaped flask. The water extracts from both cold and hot extractions (approximately 21.5 mL) were subsequently eluted through the columns in 200 μL portions without prior acidification to prevent potential racemization of the α-amino acids (Section 1.5). One milliliter of water was used to wash the walls of the columns. The resulting eluate was collected in a separate 25 mL pear-shaped flask, as it was not expected to contain sugars or amino acids, the latter of which should remain retained onto the column. Finally, to recover the amino acid fraction, 18 × 1 mL of NH3 (aq) 2 M were eluted through the column and collected in a third 25 mL pear-shaped flask.

Pre-concentration and drying. The resulting sugar and amino acid fractions from the Orgueil sample and the procedural blank without matrix were then pre-concentrated to a final volume of ~100 μL using a rotary evaporator. For this, the pressure was gradually reduced from 500 mbar to a final pressure of 25 mbar (25 °C) for the sugar fraction and 20 mbar for the amino acid fraction (26–27 °C). Each concentrated fraction was transferred to a separate 1 mL V-Vial, and the pear-shaped flasks were rinsed with 3 × 150 μL of H2O to recover any remaining analyte from the inner walls of the flasks. Finally, the samples were dried under a gentle flow of nitrogen before compound-specific derivatization. While the amino acid fraction could be dried to completion within approximately 3 h, the presence of matrix components in the sugar fraction delayed drying to up to 6 h and likely resulted in residual water remaining in the matrix (Supplementary Note 3).

Identification and quantification by enantioselective two-dimensional gas chromatography
Derivatization. The sugar fractions of the extracted samples and procedural blanks were derivatized into methylboronic acid esters following the protocol of Garcia et al.47. This involved adding 30 μL of a methylboronic acid (MBA) solution (10 mg mL–1 in pyridine) to the dried samples, vigorous vortex-mixing and heating at 60 °C for 30 min. After cooling for 10 min, the samples were then dried under a gentle stream of nitrogen, leaving approximately 2–3 μL of solvent to prevent the loss of volatile derivatives. Finally, the MBA derivatives were dissolved in 30 μL of ethyl acetate containing methyl laurate (ML) as an internal standard at a concentration of 10–6 M. Amino acids were derivatized into N-trifluoroacetyl-O-methyl (N-TFA-O-Me) esters following the protocol of Pepino et al.48. First, 120 μL of a methanol/acetyl chloride (MeOH/AcCl) solution (4:1, v/v) were added, and the mixture was vigorously stirred and heated at 110 °C for 1 h. After cooling for 10 min, the sample was dried under a gentle stream of nitrogen, leaving approximately 2 μL of solvent to prevent the loss of volatile derivatives. Next, 120 μL of a dichloromethane/trifluoroacetic acid anhydride (DCM/TFAA) solution (4:1, v/v) was added, stirred for 10 s, and heated at 100 °C for 20 min. The solution was then cooled and fully dried with nitrogen. Finally, the N-TFA-O-Me ester derivatives were dissolved in 30 μL of chloroform containing ML as an internal standard at a concentration of 10–6 M.

Analysis. The sugar and amino acid fractions from the Orgueil sample were analyzed using comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography coupled with reflectron time-of-flight mass spectrometry (GC×GC–TOF-MS) equipped with a dual-stage thermal jet modulator (Pegasus BT 4D, Leco Corp.). The injector and ion source temperatures were maintained at 230 °C, while the transfer line was set to 240 °C. Aliquots of 1 μL were injected in splitless mode. Hydrogen was used as carrier gas at a constant flow rate of 1.2 mL min–1. After each injection, the sample GC vial was immediately recapped and stored at 4 °C to prevent degradation of the amino acid and sugar derivatives before subsequent injections.

For sugar analysis, the GC×GC column configuration consisted of a CP-Chirasil-Dex CB primary column (27.15 m length × 0.25 mm inner diameter (ID), 0.25 μm film thickness, Agilent Technologies) coupled to a DB-WAX secondary column (1.61 m × 0.1 mm ID, 0.1 μm film thickness, Agilent Technologies). The primary oven was programmed as follows: an initial hold at 55 °C for 1 min, followed by a temperature increase of 10 °C min–1 to 90 °C, where it was held for 8 min. The temperature then increased at 2 °C min–1 to 190 °C, with a final isothermal hold at 190 °C for 15 min. The secondary oven and thermal modulator maintained constant positive temperature offsets of 30 °C and 15 °C, respectively. A modulation period of 5 s was applied. The reflectron TOF-MS operated at a 150 Hz storage rate, with a mass range of 50–500 amu and a microchannel plate detector voltage of approximately 2 kV and a solvent delay of 10 min.

For amino acid analysis, the column set-up included a Lipodex E primary column (24.95 m length × 0.25 mm inner diameter, Macherey-Nagel) coupled with a DB-WAX secondary column (1.7 m length × 0.12 mm inner diameter, 0.1 μm film thickness, Agilent). The primary oven was programmed as follows: an initial hold at 40 °C for 1 min, then heated to 80 °C at 10 °C min–1, holding for 10 min. The temperature was then increased to 120 °C at 1.3 °C min–1, followed by an increase to 152 °C at 0.8 °C min–1, and finally raised to 185 °C at 10 °C min–1, where it was held for 10 min. The secondary oven was operated with a constant positive temperature offset of 35 °C, and the thermal modulator hot jets had a temperature offset of 15 °C. The modulation period was 6 s. The reflectron TOF-MS operated at a 150 Hz storage rate, with a mass range of 40–500 amu, a microchannel plate detector voltage of approximately 2 kV, and a solvent delay of 9 min.

Analyte identification was performed by comparing retention times across both chromatographic dimensions and mass spectra (within a 500-ppm mass tolerance) with a mixed analyte standard. Quantification was performed using four-point calibration curves for the target analytes ranging from 5 × 10–8 M to 10–6 M, with manual integration conducted via LECO Corp. ChromaTOF™ software.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Review comments on NCOMMS-25-43746
Overall: The paper by Leyva et al. reported the detection of sugars in the samples returned from the asteroid (162173)
Ryugu, as well as that in Orgueil meteorites. The authors utilized an ultrasonic-assisted extraction and a stereoselective
analytical method using GCxGC-TOF-MS. As a result, they reported the detection of D and L-arabinose and D and L-xylose
from the extract from Ryugu. From the Orgueil extract, the detection of not only arabinose and xylose, but also other
aldopentose sugars such as ribose, lyxose, and ribulose was reported. The present results were the second detection of
abiotic aldopentose sugars in extraterrestrial samples after Furukawa et al. (2019), who confirmed the presence of
indigenous sugars based on their 13C enrichments. On the other hand, enantioselective analyses of sugars were performed
for the first time in the present study, which can, in principle, definitely distinguish between abiotic and biotic sugars.
The detection of biologically relevant molecules in extraterrestrial materials is of special interest from the viewpoint of
prebiotic evolution and the origin of life on Earth and elsewhere in the solar system. Moreover, the detection of sugars, which
may be minor in extraterrestrial materials, from tiny portions of Ryugu samples is challenging. So, the report on the
successful detection of sugars in such a tiny, valuable sample deserves publication in Nature Communications.
However, there is a critical problem in the present manuscript: a blank control was really insufficient in the present study. For
example, although significant sugar contaminants were detected in the procedural blank (PB) experiment, the authors did
not evaluate their contribution to the detected sugars in Ryugu and Orgueil. This is based on their opinion that the recovery
of sugars is poor when some mineral matrices are used. If no sugars were detected in the PB without such minerals, the
sugars detected in the sample are reasonably acceptable as indigenous to the samples. However, as long as
significant contaminations are present in the PB and no evaluation of their contributions is performed, the reported quantification values
and the enantiomeric parameters cannot be accepted as indigenous to Ryugu and Orgueil.
I guess pristine Ryugu samples are no longer available, so the reanalysis of Ryugu samples would be difficult, unfortunately.
However, according to the authors, they still have enough Orgueil meteorite samples. So, I strongly recommend authors to
evaluate the potential contamination very carefully under the same analytical conditions with the meteorite samples and to
perform extraction and analysis of sugars in Orgueil meteorites again. As for the Ryugu results, based on the new analyses
of PB and Orgueil, the presence of sugars should be evaluated in more detail, although any reliable quantification would not
be possible. I hope the following comments are helpful in improving the current manuscript.
-L8: I cannot understand the meaning of “unequal distribution”. This should be rephrased appropriately.
-L10, “robust formation of sugars in laboratory simulations of interstellar ice chemistry”: I do not think that the robust formation
of sugars in interstellar ices has been established in earlier laboratory experiments. For example, de Marcellus et al. (2015)
and Meinert et al. (2016) performed laboratory experiments at liquid-nitrogen temperature, which may be less relevant to
processes in the coldest regions in the interstellar medium (ISM), whose typical temperature is as low as 10 K. Nuevo et al.
(2018) and Zhang et al. (2024) used unrealistic ices in the ISM for the reactants (e.g., methanol and CO mixed ices, water
and methanol mixed ices, without other components). I do not doubt the formation of sugars in their experiments, but I do not
fully agree with the “robust formation of sugars” in interstellar ice chemistry.
-L13, L82-85: “ultrasonic-assisted extraction” is not a new technique for the extraction of sugars from meteorites. The
enantioselective analyses by GCxGC should be emphasized more.
-L36: Ref 13 (Yokoyama et al.) did not report the presence of amino acids and nucleobases in Ryugu.
-L40-42: What is the meaning of “a significant gap”? It does not make sense if the authors expect the possible formation of
sugars in laboratory experiments under the simulated ISM or parent body conditions. As pointed out above, laboratory
experiments did not necessarily simulate the actual conditions in extraterrestrial environments. Moreover, not only the
formation of sugars (refs. 16-22) but also their degradation event should have taken place in each environment. Without
considering both effects, the expression “significant gap” is too strong.
L56-60: “This concern ... sample processing.” These sentences should be deleted because they would give a negative
impression to readers, as if all returned samples have been contaminated. Even without these sentences, it makes sense to
readers.
L71-73: As for arabinose in NWA 801, Furukawa et al. (2019) did not report the d13C value due to the significant
contribution by the co-eluting peak. However, they also claimed that arabinose and ribose in Murchison and ribose in NWA
801 are not significantly affected by their co-eluting peaks. It seems to me that the sentence here is based on the current
author’s subjective opinions only. Hence, the sentence in Lines 71-73 should be deleted.
L87: This should be deleted since this is a repetitive sentence of L80-82.
L90-92: This sentence is too strong since it is just based on the author’s assumption.
L103: Which previous studies do the authors point out? Cite some references here.
L119: “MBA” is appropriate as an abbreviation of methyl boronate?
L124, “significantly above the procedural blank levels”: This sentence is overstated.
L128, “near-racemic ratio (D/L ~ 1.0)”: This sentence is also overstated since no blank control has been done.
Figure 2: In the PB data, not only L-Ara but also D-Ara (~34.10 for 1D, =1.8 for 2D) should be present, although the peak
intensities vary significantly between D and L enantiomers, possibly due to the biological contamination of L-Ara and the
contamination from the standard reagent of D-Ara (if the authors use the “expansion” technique as used in Figure 6a, this
peak should be observed more clearly). The presence of D-Ara in PB should be evaluated in more detail. Since the range of

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Major comments:
This research investigated sugars in the sample of the carbonaceous asteroid Ryugu. The sample is extremely valuable,
and the chiral separation of sugars represents a significant novel development. Thus, this research is suitable for
consideration in Nature Communications. However, I have several concerns with this analysis, primarily related to the
potential contamination of biological and unclear sources of sugars, which may be derived from a standard chemical
mixture. Suppose this contamination occurred outside of the sample solution, such as in the GC-MS injector. In that case, a
repeat analysis of the sample with a clean GC-MS system will provide a convincing result. However, if this contamination
occurred in the sample solution, I have no idea how to show the presence of extraterrestrial sugars in the Ryugu with this
sample. Thus, the manuscript, at least in this form, is not sufficient to show that the Ryugu sample contains abiotic sugars.
1. The central issue is the contamination of both D-sugars and L-sugars in the sample of Orgueil and potentially Ryugu. In
this type of analysis, the procedural blank that undergoes the same conditions as the sample is crucial for demonstrating
contamination. The procedural blank of Orgueil shows contamination of D-ribose, L-ribose, D-lyxose, and L-lyxose. Since L-
ribose and L-lyxose are not biological contaminants, this suggests that cross-contamination of the standard or sample
occurred with the procedural blank. I guess the contamination was from the standard because the significantly higher
abundance of ribose and lyxose than arabinose and xylose is not reasonable as abiotic sugars, and the relative abundance
between sugars is different from that of the Orgueil. Given the presence of cross-contamination, the chromatogram of the
Orgueil sample may be consistent with the sugar composition of the standard + biological contaminants. The author should
explain considering this possibility, both in Ryugu and Orgueil. To discuss this possibility, the authors should show the
chromatogram of the standard mixture.
2. The amounts of D-xylose and L-arabinose in the procedural blank for the Ryugu sample should be listed in the Table. The
abundance of D-xylose in Ryugu maybe comparable to that detected in the procedural blank. They should be compared.
3. L268-269 and table 1: The authors describe that “Among these, ribose, lyxose, and ribulose showed racemic distributions,
consistent with an extraterrestrial origin.” However, near-racemic ribose and lyxose are also detected in the procedural
blank, indicating that the detected ribose and lyxose are possible contaminants from the standard. If we suppose that the
amounts of D-arabinose and L-xylose are authigenic of Orgueil, why do ribose and lyxose (rare sugar) have 20-30 times
greater amounts? As the author shows, the recovery of ribose is only 4%, indicating that ribose is present at a concentration
more than 300 times that of arabinose. This is not reasonable. The compositions of sugars in the procedural blank implies
that the same source of contamination occurred more significantly to Orgueil.
4. The data on ribulose is missing. This should be shown.
5. The chromatograms and abundance of ribose and lyxose in Ryugu should be shown.
6. The authors underlined the novelty and advantage of this extraction repeatedly. However, the ultrasonic-assisted room
temperature extraction has been conducted in previous studies with water and 2% HCl (Cooper et al. 2001 and Furukawa et
al., 2019). The clear difference in this study is extraction by methanol. However, extraction of sugars with methanol is not
effective, owing to their low solubility compared to water and HCl. For example, Alessandro et al., (Alessandro C. Galvão,
Maicon R. Zangalli, Pedro Felipe Arce, Weber S. Robazza, Solubility of fructose and sucrose in mixtures of methanol and
water: Experiment and application of equations of state and activity coefficient model, Journal of Food Engineering, 369,
2024,) shows that the solubility of fructose in methanol is less than 10% in water. The loss of the extraction is evaluated in
this method using the addition of sugars to Orgueil. Thus, this is not an essential problem, but clearly this extraction is not the
advantage but disadvantage from previous studies.
7. The table 2 shows the abundance of amino acids and their blank-subtracted values. The values of “UNH(a)” represent
sample + contaminants and the value with “UNH(b)” are real extraterrestrial amino acids. Many of the values in “b” is n.v.,
meaning that they are smaller than the blank. This means that the procedural blank does not work as procedural blank.
8. The manuscript should show reproducibility of amino acid analysis. If they consider the reproducibility, several values in
the “b” column may be not reliable. For example, D-Ala was detected in the sample and blank at 0.326 and 0.378,
respectively. If the reproducibility is 10%, the difference is not clear. This may happen also for 2-ABA.
9. The amounts of amino acids in the procedural blank for Orgueil should be shown in the table.
10. Any meteorite has the potential for contamination from sampling to curation. To prevent this effect in previous studies of
sugars, meteorites were trimmed to remove potentially contaminated surfaces (Cooper et al. 2001 and Furukawa et al.,
2019). Did the authors trim Orgueil to remove contamination, or did the authors use an inner part of the original fragment of
Orgueil? The data of Orgueil analysis in this manuscript shows contamination of biological sugars and amino acids. If they
analyzed with exposed surface, this could be the primary reason of biological contamination.
Specific comments:
Abstract: The present data set shown in the manuscript does not sufficiently represent the presence of extraterrestrial sugars.
The color code for the sample and procedural blank should be within the same range, from 0 to the maximum, to allow
readers to compare them. For example, Fig 1 A and B should be from 0 (blue) to 300000 (red).
The total 2D chromatograms covering all investigated sugars for samples, blanks, and the standard should be shown. The
present manuscript contains only Orgueil and its procedural blank (Fig. 4).
L57: Even though there is some potential for the microbial colonization of Ryugu sample, the evidence is poor in this cited
paper limited in shape, which can be formed by withering. Also, this potential contamination happened in the allocated
sample by the researchers which means that the allocated sample was not contaminated. The present explanation is
confusing.
L102-103: The author explained here that “Key to this methodology is a mild extraction protocol that replaces conventional
high-temperature acid hydrolysis with milder ultrasonic-assisted extraction to prevent thermal degradation of sugars.”
However, this is not correct. The previous sugar extraction was conducted at room temperature with water (Cooper et al.,
2001) or 2% HCl, which is lower concentration than amino acid hydrolysis (Furukawa et al., 2019) with sonication. Thus,
ultrasonic-assisted mild extraction is not new.
L123: The manuscript describes that “we unambiguously detected both enantiomers of arabinose and xylose in Ryugu
extracts at concentrations significantly above the procedural blank level.” However, the amounts of arabinose and xylose in
the procedural blank are not shown in the manuscript. Figures 2 and 3 clearly show that there are larger amounts of L-
arabinose and D-xylose in the procedural blank than in the Ryugu sample. So, the description in the manuscript is not
correct. The 3D peaks of D-arabinose and L-xylose look larger in Ryugu than the procedural blank, but these peaks in
Ryugu are magnified in these figures. So, the figure does not provide information on their amounts.
In the revised manuscript, the amounts of both D and L arabinose and xylose in the procedural blank should be shown in
Table 1 and explained based on these amounts.
L128: The manuscript explains that arabinose in Ryugu has a D/L approximately 1.0. However, Table 1 shows that the D/L
of arabinose in Ryugu is 0.727. They are not racemic, but D-rich.
Table 1: The manuscript explains in L 142 that “D-arabinose and L-xylose as ~0.01 nmol/g and ~0.001 nmol/g, respectively”.
These values would not be consistent with the data in Table.
L145-146: The manuscript discusses that the lower abundance of contaminants in Ryugu than PB was caused by the
adsorption by minerals. In this case, what was the source of the contamination? Did the authors analyze solvents every time
before the analysis of the sample and PB? If so, please describe this to eliminate the possibility of cross-contamination in
GC-MS. Otherwise, the cross-contamination may explain the chromatogram of Ryugu (real Ryugu+PB) or (PB+standard).
The PB of Orgueil shown in Fig. 4 shows that D- and L-lyxose and D- and L-ribose are contaminated. D- and L-lyxose are
rare sugars and L-ribose is non-biological sugar. Thus, they could not be biological contaminations. So, they could be
contaminated from the standard chemical mixture in the GC-MS. If this happened in the Ryugu sample. The presence of L-
xylose and D-arabinose could be explained by this effect. The authors should show the analytical blank before the Ryugu
analysis.
L167: The chromatograms of ribulose should be shown in the manuscript.
L167: The author should show chromatograms of Orgueil, procedural blank, and the standard of ribulose.
L172-175: The author discussed that acid extraction of sugars from Murchison reported in Furukawa et al. (2019) may
introduce sugar contamination and promote sugar formation reaction. However, in the previous study, the paper described
no detectable pentose contamination in the procedural blank. Thus, the contamination from 2% HCl in the extraction is
unfounded.
Further, sugar formation by the formose reaction is highly sensitive to high pH, indicating that low pH is more suitable for
extraction. The higher stabilities of sugars at lower pH are also evident in other previous study, in which the
degradation of ribose is 100 times lower at pH4.5 compared to 6.5 (Larralde et al., 1995).
Thus, this discussion should be removed.
L244-245: Arabinose in Ryugu is enriched in L-form.
L293: The author discussed that abundant ammonia stabilized sugars, by maintaining pH for optimal aldol condensation.
However, this is not correct. Ammonia react with sugars to form may by-products (e.g., Kebukawa et al., Science Advances
2017). Further, aldol condensation promoted by high pH consume sugars as shown in many previous studies including the
author’s work (Vinogradoff et al., 2024).
Figure 2-6: Do the 2D and 3D chromatograms show total ion chromatograms or selected ion chromatograms? This should
be explained in the caption with m/z range or m/z values.
Figure 4 and 5: The assignment of D-arabinose is different between Figure 4 and 5.
Minor comments:
L28: Proteins are better described as catalytic biopolymers rather than informational biopolymers, since the term
informational biopolymers is widely used to express the biopolymers that have gene information.
L80-97: These paragraphs mostly describe results and implications. Thus, they should be merged in the
following section.
L82: ribuloses to ribulose
L98: The title of this section should be “Results and Discussion”
L118: “as well as the the C5 ketose” to “as well as the C5 ketose”
L155: (PB) to (B)
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Below you will find my review of manuscript NCOMMS-25-43746 entitled “Abiotic sugars in 9162173) Ryugu and the
primitive CI carbonaceous chondrite Orgueil” and submitted to Nature Communications.
Overall this manuscript is very interesting. The results presented are important to the astrobiology and planetary science
communities, and timely given the ongoing studies and publications related to the analyses of samples from asteroids
Ryugu and Bennu. There are, however, a few things about that manuscript that bother me, and I would like the authors to
consider my comments below before I can recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature Communications.
General comments:
The thing that bothers me the most about this manuscript is the strange imbalance between the study of sugars and that of
amino acids. On the one hand, the title of manuscript only refers to the detection of sugars in Ryugu and Orgueil samples,
but on the other hand, half of the paper is dedicated to the detection of amino acids. Indeed, the Results, Discussion, and
Methods section all significantly describe the protocol, detection, and data interpretation of amino acids in those samples at
almost the same level as for sugars. In particular, Tables 2 and 3 are huge and only related to amino acids. But somehow
the title doesn’t mention anything about amino acids at all.
I do acknowledge and appreciate the fact that the authors included detailed protocol and results obtained for the detection of
amino acids in both Ryugu and Orgueil samples, and I understand that this information helps (1) compare the results
presented in this manuscript with previous studies, and (2) assess the origin and level of contamination of the samples for
both amino acids and sugars, i.e., extraterrestrial vs. terrestrial contamination.
However, this makes the actual objective of this manuscript confusing, to say the least. Is the manuscript about the detection
of sugars (as the title suggests) or about the detection of both sugars and amino acids? Was this manuscript originally two
separate manuscripts that eventually ended up stitched together, because some information from the study of amino acids
could help support the extraterrestrial origin of sugars?
In addition, there are two statements in the manuscript that are not supported by any of the figures nor the tables:
Claim 1: The manuscript clearly mentions several times the (first reported) detection of ribulose in both Ryugu and Orgueil
samples. However, there are no figures to support this claim anywhere. At the very least, this claim should be supported by a
figure with GCxGC-TOFMS data (chromatograms + mass spectra) showing the detection of ribulose and a comparison with
the procedural blank and the reference standard, similarly to other detected sugars. As is, the authors are asking the readers
to accept the first detection of ribulose in extraterrestrial samples on a “trust me when we tell you” basis.
Claim 2: Similarly, there are no supporting figures for the detections of the amino acids mentioned in the manuscript. I
understand that the current version of the manuscript wants to focus on the detection of sugars (see my other general
comments above), but at the same time the authors make many claims regarding the detection of several amino acids, use
those data to determine enantiomeric excesses and to show that the amino acid data support an extraterrestrial origin for
both the sugars and amino acids detected here. Therefore, supporting the claims of detection of amino acids is critical to the
message this manuscript wants to convey and, like the detection of ribulose, these detections can’t be based only on good
faith.
Finally, I am a bit concerned about the levels of contamination in the procedural blanks (PBs). Indeed, Figures 2, 3, and 5
show high levels of contamination for the compounds (both sugars and amino acids) that the authors are searching for in the
samples. For example, the intensity of the peak for L-Ara in the PB shown in Figure 2 is over 7 times higher than the intensity
of the peak for L-Ara in the Ryugu sample. Similarly, the intensity of the peak for D-Xyl in the PB shown in Figure 2 is
comparable to the intensity of the peak for D-Xyl in the Ryugu sample. I understand that other elements of the analysis still
point towards an extraterrestrial origin of these compounds, but this is quite concerning, and the authors should provide a
more solid explanation of why these abundant contaminants are still consistent with an extraterrestrial origin for these
sugars. On a similar topic, why were the values reported in Tables 1, 2, and 3 for the abundances of sugars and amino acids
in both Ryugu and Orgueil not corrected for PBs? How can the abundances and enantiomeric excesses found for the
detected compounds be compared with previous studies if the values used for these determinations are not
corrected?
In summary, some decisions need to be made by the authors regarding the revisions to this manuscript. I see 2 possible
options:
Option 1: The authors could almost entirely remove the text and parts of the figures regarding the study of amino acids, and
publish those very interesting results in a separate paper. In this case, they could easily add the GCxGC-TOFMS data
missing to support the detection of ribulose, expand the discussion regarding the contaminants seen in the PBs, and decide
what to do with the uncorrected values reported in Table 1.
Option 2: The authors could officially make this manuscript a study of the detection of both sugars and amino acids in Ryugu
and Orgueil. To this purpose, they would need to add figures showing GCxGC-TOFMS data for amino acids to support their
detection claims, expand the discussion regarding the contaminants seen in the PBs, and decide what to do with the
uncorrected values reported in Tables 1, 2, and 3. This option may however result in a significant increase of the length of
the manuscript.
Other more specific, minor comments:
Title: As mentioned in my general comments, the fact that the title only mentions the detection of sugars while a lot of the text
and the tables provided in the manuscript are about the detection of amino acids and their enantiomeric excesses is strange.
In the case the authors choose to fully add all the information regarding the analysis of amino acids in the manuscript,
including the actual GCxGC-TOFMS data, then the title should be modified accordingly.
Title: Another small detail that bothers me in the title is the specific mention of “primitive” to qualify the Orgueil meteorite.
This is a bit in contradiction with what is mentioned in the manuscript, when it is said that meteorites that are collected on
the Earth’s surface, such as Orgueil, are more prone to contamination because they have been in contact with potential
contaminants. In that sense, even if the original piece of rock that fell from the sky, and was later named “Orgueil meteorite”,
originated from a primitive parent body (probably an asteroid), it is strange to specify that Orgueil is a primitive meteorite,
while the samples collected from Ryugu are probably more primitive than any meteorite collected on Earth.
Lines 33–34: I often see a phrase in the introductions of papers stating that exogeneous organic materials are probably
delivered by extraterrestrial objects such as meteorites and interplanetary dust particles (IDPs). Is there any actual published
study that shows the detection of extraterrestrial organic compounds such as amino acids and sugars in IDPs?
Line 36: The “the” before “asteroids” is unnecessary.
Lines 44–45: I don’t understand how the RNA world hypothesis has anything to do with the critical goal to investigate the
formation of sugars. Even if the RNA world hypothesis turns out to be wrong, the fact that sugars are used in RNA and DNA
in all modern biological systems is the main motivation for studying the origin and formation of sugars from an astrobiological
point of view, no matter an actual RNA world played a role in the history of biological evolution or not.
Lines 50–52: This sentence has a negative connotation, as if only the detection of sugars in extraterrestrial materials
mattered. Is the presence or detection of sugar alcohols and/or sugar acids in extraterrestrial materials really a bad thing?
Even if sugars are converted into their alcohol and/or acid derivatives, their presence is also interesting, because they may
provide important information about the conditions (temperature, pH, precursors, etc.) under which sugar derivatives in
general were formed in the parent bodies, and because they can still be converted back to sugars under conditions that may
have existed on the surface or in the oceans of the early Earth.
Line 57: Add “to” after “prior”: “prior to analysis”.
Line 59: Add “JAXA” before “Hayabusa2” and “NASA” before “OSIRIS-REx”.
Line 64: The reference numbers after “O” look confusing because they come right after “13C” and “15N”. Moreover, although
the isotopes of interest for carbon and nitrogen are specified (13C and 15N), those for oxygen are missing (18O?). In any
case, in particular if the isotopic number is added to O, the references should be provided in a less confusing format, e.g.,
“(refs. 36–38)”.
Line 122: It should be spelled “extraterrestrial” (no hyphen).
Line 124: Figures 2 and 3 don’t display any “resolutions”, but they do display “chromatograms” or more precisely “2D-chromatograms”.
Captions of Figures 2, 3, 5, and 6: It is obvious that “RS” in the bottom 2D-chromatograms stands for “reference standard”,
but it is not explicitly defined anywhere, in contrast to “PB” for “procedural blank”, which is explicitly defined.
Line 166: I defy anybody to be able to use the data used in Figure 4 to conclude that lyxose is detected in nearly racemic
conditions. It’s impossible to see that from the information provided in Figure 4.
Line 214: N-methylglycine is indeed used in biological systems, but it’s not a proteinogenic amino acid.
Line 215: Per IUPAC convention, the “allo” in “allo-isoleucine” should be in italics.
Line 220: The comma after “content” is unnecessary.
Lines 250–252: These sentences are a near word-for-word repetition of text provided earlier and don’t belong to the
Discussion section.
Line 256: Re-order the words as: “CI (Ivuna-like) chondrites”.
Line 260: “solar system” should be capitalized: “Solar System”.
Lines 292–294: I disagree with point (3). Too much NH3 in the system would result in higher amounts of N atoms
incorporated into organic compounds, which would inhibit the formation of sugars and sugar derivatives and favor the
formation of N-bearing compounds instead.
Line 324: I believe there’s a typo and it should be “Class II” (no space).
Line 338: I would add a hyphen between “pre” and “treatment”: “pre-treatment”.
Lines 352, 355, and 358: Those steps all mention water extractions, but no information is provided regarding the origin and
purity of water. I know that this information is provided in detail in the Supplementary Information, but I still think it should be
mentioned here at least once that the water used is water filtered to a purity of 18.2 MΩ cm.
Line 374: I believe that Nature Communications follows British English spelling, and therefore the correct spelling should be
“millilitre”.
Line 398: From the context, I can guess that “MBA” refers to “methylboronic acid”, as it should have been defined on line
396.
Line 399: Inversely, the abbreviation “ML” for “methyl laurate” is defined here but never used again afterwards, even though
“methyl laurate” is mentioned again on line 407, where the abbreviation could have been used but wasn’t.
Table 1: No matter how loosely I interpret the numbers reported in the table, I can’t seem to find a value of 95.3% for the eeD
of xylose in Orgueil from the abundances provided for L- and D-xylose (0.22 and 3.22, respectively). For example, if I
assume that 0.22 and 3.22 were rounded from 0.215 and 3.224 (extreme numbers that would still be rounded up to those
provided in the table), the resulting eeD is 86.7%, which is still well under the 95.3% value reported in the table. Therefore, I
don’t understand where these 95.3% come from.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: Thank you for your overall positive and encouraging evaluation of our manuscript, as well
as for your insightful remarks, which have clearly helped us to refine and strengthen the work. We
fully acknowledge the challenges in unequivocally confirming the presence of extraterrestrial sugars
in such samples—particularly in the case of Ryugu, where the quantities available are extremely
limited. We have now included in the manuscript a thorough study targeting the identification of the
sources of sugar contamination in our analyses. Distinct enantiomeric composition of arabinose in the
Ryugu fragments compared to our procedural blanks strongly supports different origin of at least some
of arabinose detected in the Ryugu sample. Furthermore, the near-racemic ratios of some of the
amino acids found in the Ryugu fragments can be taken as a precedent for the extraterrestrial origin
of at least some of the arabinose detected in the Ryugu extracts. In the case of xylose, the results
remain more elusive, which we now clearly state in the manuscript. Since our spiking experiments
clearly demonstrate the negative impact of the meteorite matrix on sugar recovery, and given that
the SiO₂ used in our procedural blanks does not adequately replicate the complex nature of the Ryugu
or Orgueil matrices, we chose not to apply blank corrections to the absolute quantities or
enantiomeric excess values of sugars detected in the extraterrestrial samples, as such corrections
could bias the results in an unknown manner. Rather than applying corrections, we present the
absolute values of sugar contents in the Ryugu and Orgueil samples, with the caution that our
discussion should be considered when interpreting these preliminary quantitative data.
For better comparison with the existing literature on amino acids in Ryugu and Orgueil, we followed
common practice and report now both the ‘absolute’ and procedural blank–corrected quantities
(Table 1). However, we strongly caution that these absolute values should be interpreted carefully,
given the current limitations of the procedural blanks typically employed in the research community.
Detailed studies of the impact of the meteorite matrix, that are beyond the scope of the present
manuscript, are necessary to develop standardized protocols for blank-corrections in the future. These
should be then employed throughout all studies in the community to facilitate quantitative
comparisons between organics contained in distinct parent bodies. We expand on the above-
mentioned points in more detail in the point-by-point responses below.
Revised in the manuscript: Table 1: blank-corrected quantities for amino acids in Ryugu and Orgueil.
-L8: I cannot understand the meaning of “unequal distribution”. This should be rephrased
appropriately.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity in our use of the term “unequal
distribution.” To improve clarity, we have revised the sentence to more accurately reflect the
observed variability in detection and abundance of different compound classes.
The revised sentence in the manuscript now reads: “The uneven detection of prebiotic organic
compounds in meteorites—where amino acids and nucleobases are frequently identified, while sugars
are rarely detected and remain poorly characterized.“
-L10, “robust formation of sugars in laboratory simulations of interstellar ice chemistry”: I do not think
that the robust formation of sugars in interstellar ices has been established in earlier laboratory
experiments. For example, de Marcellus et al. (2015) and Meinert et al. (2016) performed laboratory
experiments at liquid-nitrogen temperature, which may be less relevant to processes in the coldest
regions in the interstellar medium (ISM), whose typical temperature is as low as 10 K. Nuevo et al.

2 2

adaptation of the temperature programme of the secondary oven was necessary to keep optimal

subsequent pre-treatment and GC-MS analysis, we introduced an additional purification barrier by
increasing the quantity of resin and including a polyethersulfone (PES) syringe filter.

6. The authors underlined the novelty and advantage of this extraction repeatedly. However, the
ultrasonic-assisted room temperature extraction has been conducted in previous studies with water
and 2% HCl (Cooper et al. 2001 and Furukawa et al., 2019). The clear difference in this study is

low solubility compared to water and HCl. For example, Alessandro et al., (Alessandro C. Galvão,
Maicon R. Zangalli, Pedro Felipe Arce, Weber S. Robazza, Solubility of fructose and sucrose in mixtures
of methanol and water: Experiment and application of equations of state and activity coefficient
model, Journal of Food Engineering, 369, 2024,) shows that the solubility of fructose in methanol is less

advantage but disadvantage from previous studies.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. While the reviewer cites studies on the
solubility limit of C6 fructose and sucrose disaccharide in methanol, these sugars were not the target
of our analysis. We focused on small C3-C5 sugars which are highly soluble in methanol. In addition,
our target analytes are trace-level meteoritic sugars, with expected concentrations many orders of
magnitude below solubility limits of these sugars in methanol. Even with its lower solubility, methanol
can dissolve micromolar or nanomolar quantities of sugars with ease. Importantly, we selected
methanol as the extraction solvent for sugars because it has several analytical advantages over water.
Methanol has been shown to limit the extraction of inorganic ions from the meteorite matrix
(Timoumi et al. Ultrasonics Sonochemistry 103, 106775 (2025)—reducing interference during
downstream analyses—while effectively solubilizing a broad range of polar organic compounds,
including sugar-related molecules
In an FT-ICR mass spectrometry study of the Murchison meteorite, methanol extracts yielded
significantly more CHO-containing molecular formulas than water extractions—demonstrating its
superior efficiency for extracting soluble polar organics (including polyols) while minimizing matrix-
derived salts (Schmitt-Kopplin et al. PNAS 107, 2763 (2010)). Furthermore, Schmitt-Kopplin et al.
(2023) demonstrated that methanol extracts from Ryugu contained abundant CHO-rich and polyol-
like compounds, reinforcing its suitability for targeting sugars in extraterrestrial materials
(https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-42075-y)
We consider, therefore, that the use of methanol is an "advantage" and not a disadvantage of our
method as it is more compatible with salt-sensitive analytical workflows. Nevertheless, in view of the
low overall sugar recoveries, we intend to test alternative extraction protocols in future work and will
incorporate the reviewer’s advice into our experimental design.

(162173) Ryugu and the primitive CI carbonaceous chondrite Orgueil” resubmitted to Nature

Despite of all the justified explanations and subsequent significant changes made to the revised
version of the manuscript, I still can’t recommend this manuscript for publication in Nature
Communications. Below I provide a more detail argumentation that led to my decision. That being
said, this doesn’t mean that I don’t recommend this manuscript for publication at all. The work
presented here is important and show novel results that deserve to be published (in a different
journal) and shared with the scientific community.
I totally understand the arguments presented by the authors to defend the data reported in the
manuscript, and I fully appreciate the difficulty to obtain these data given the limited quantities of
materials they had to work with. On the other hand, the long replies from the authors to the
comments of all three reviewers all seem to point towards the fact that, given the data collected for
the sample of Ryugu that was analyzed in this study, given the low recovery rate for the extraction of
sugars from the mineral matrix, and given the analytical protocol resulting in the contamination of
the samples, and consequently the results presented in the manuscript, there is currently no way to
know for sure that the sugars identified in the chromatograms of this Ryugu sample are indigenous to
Ryugu.
I understand that the data collected for amino acids as well as the distribution of sugars in the
samples compared with the procedural blank (PB) data suggest an indigenous origin from Ryugu,
because their enantiomeric distributions are different from that of the PBs, but they don’t provide a
definitive proof. In particular, the fact that quantitative amounts and enantiomeric excess
measurements can’t be corrected using the PBs makes the detection of both amino acids and sugars
inconclusive. Believe me, I really want these compounds to be indigenous to Ryugu, and I think their
unambiguous presence would be a great result, but the data shown in the manuscript are currently
insufficient to unambiguously confirm these detections. I understand that the detection of amino
acids in Ryugu in the present study supports an extraterrestrial origin for these compounds. However,

addition, since the extraction protocols are different for amino acids and sugars, even if amino acids
are indigenous to Ryugu, this doesn’t mean that sugars are, because different extraction solvents can
contain different levels of amino acid and sugar contaminants.
Therefore, I don’t think the data and results presented in this manuscript are strong enough to
convince everybody that sugars were detected in Ryugu without any possible doubt, and I believe that
publications in Nature Communications should show results that are proof-tight and totally
unambiguous, which is not the case here.

important and they should be published. Given that in their responses to the reviewers, the authors
mentioned at multiple occasions that they are currently working on a separate manuscript in which
they will address the development of the protocol for the simultaneous analysis of amino acids and
sugars, as well as the impact of the mineral matrix on their recoveries, I suggest that the authors

amino acids and sugars, their extraction protocol, the impact of the mineral matrix, and a more
comprehensive discussion of the interpretation of these results after addressing the contamination

stronger arguments for the origin of the amino acids and sugars detected in the Ryugu sample

significant contribution to the scientific community.

Review comments on the manuscript #NCOMMS-25-43746B by Meinert et al.
Overall:

comparison with other meteorites/asteroids, should be discussed much more.

taking into account the above and the following concerns. Please accept my apologies that some of the
questions and opinions below may not have been communicated to the authors in earlier rounds of
review, which primarily focused on the justification of the Ryugu results.
1. L38, “only a single study by Furukawa et al. has confirmed that...”: Very recently, as the authors may
have already known, a paper on the detection of sugars in the sample returned from the asteroid Bennu

aldopentoses detected in Bennu into Table 1, allowing a more direct comparison with our data from

for the broad audience of Nature Communications, we have chosen not to include further
methodological details in the main text. We note that a more technical investigation of aldopentose
recovery and degradation kinetics under our analytical conditions is ongoing and will be reported
separately.
6. L180-: What kind of “sugar-specific” interactions did the authors find? Please clarify.

Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. By “sugar-specific interactions,” we
refer to the distinct and reproducible differences observed among individual aldopentoses in both

Table 1, the measured recovery rates differ significantly between ribose, arabinose, xylose, and lyxose,

and/or extraction protocol. In addition, Supplementary Fig. 10 demonstrates sugar-dependent
degradation patterns, with individual aldopentoses exhibiting markedly different stability profiles

differential, sugar-specific interactions with the mineral matrix and/or during analytical handling,

distinction in terms of biological relevance and therefore help to distinguish potential sources of
contamination. Proteinogenic amino acids are those directly encoded by the genetic code and
incorporated into proteins by ribosomal translation in extant biology. Rare (non-proteinogenic but
biological) amino acids are compounds that occur naturally in terrestrial biological systems but are
not encoded by the standard genetic code. These include amino acids found in specialized metabolic
